title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: The floor of the stage consisted of smooth boards, with some painted cardboard representing trees at the sides, and at the back a cloth stretched over boards. In the center of the stage sat some girls in red bodices and white skirts. One very fat girl in a white silk dress sat apart on a low bench, to the back of which a piece of green cardboard was glued. They all sang something. When they had finished their song, the girl in white went up to the prompter's box, and a man in tight silk trousers over his stout legs, holding a plume and a dagger, went up to her and began singing, waving his arms about.

First the man in the tight trousers sang alone, then she sang, then they both paused while the orchestra played and the man fingered the hand of the girl in white, clearly waiting for the beat to start singing with her. They sang together and everyone in the theater began clapping and shouting, while the man and woman on the stage — who were supposed to be lovers — began smiling, spreading out their arms, and bowing.

After her life in the country and in her present serious mood, all this seemed absurd and bizarre to Natasha. She couldn't follow the opera or even listen to the music; she saw only the painted cardboard and the strangely dressed men and women who moved, spoke, and sang so oddly in that brilliant light. She knew what it was all supposed to represent, but it was so pretentiously false and unnatural that she first felt embarrassed for the actors and then amused by them. She looked at the faces in the audience, seeking the same sense of ridiculousness and confusion she herself was feeling, but they all seemed absorbed in what was happening on stage and expressed a delight that seemed to Natasha completely fake. "I suppose it has to be like this!" she thought. She kept looking around at the rows of groomed heads in the stalls and then at the half-dressed women in the boxes, especially at Helene in the next box, who — apparently almost naked — sat with a calm, peaceful smile, never taking her eyes off the stage. And feeling the bright light that flooded the whole place and the warm air heated by the crowd, Natasha gradually began to drift into a state of intoxication she hadn't experienced for a long time. She lost awareness of who and where she was, and what was going on in front of her. As she looked and thought, the strangest ideas unexpectedly and disconnectedly passed through her mind: the urge to jump onto the edge of the box and sing the aria the actress was singing, or to reach out with her fan and touch an old gentleman sitting not far from her, or to lean over to Helene and tickle her.

At a moment when everything was quiet before a new song, a door leading to the stalls on the side nearest the Rostovs' box creaked, and the steps of a late arrival were heard. "There's Kuragin!" whispered Shinshin. Countess Bezukhova turned smiling to the newcomer, and Natasha, following the direction of that look, saw an exceptionally handsome officer approaching their box with a self-assured yet courteous air. This was Anatole Kuragin, whom she had seen and noticed long ago at the ball in Petersburg. He was now in an officer's uniform with one epaulet and a shoulder knot. He moved with a restrained swagger that would have been ridiculous had he not been so good-looking and had his handsome face not worn such an expression of good-humored satisfaction and gaiety. Though the performance was going on, he walked deliberately down the carpeted aisle, his sword and spurs slightly jingling and his handsome, perfumed head held high. Having looked at Natasha, he approached his sister, laid his well-gloved hand on the edge of her box, nodded to her, and leaning forward asked a question, gesturing toward Natasha.

"Absolutely charming!" said he, clearly referring to Natasha, who didn't exactly hear his words but understood them from the movement of his lips. Then he took his seat in the first row of the stalls and sat down beside Dolokhov, nudging him in a friendly, casual way — that Dolokhov whom others treated so deferentially. He winked at him merrily, smiled, and rested his foot against the orchestra railing.
"How alike the brother and sister are," remarked the count. "And how handsome they both are!"
Shinshin, lowering his voice, began telling the count about some intrigue of Kuragin's in Moscow, and Natasha tried to overhear it just because he had called her "charming."
The first act was over. In the stalls everyone began moving about, going out and coming in.

Boris came to the Rostovs' box, accepted their congratulations very simply, and raising his eyebrows with an absent-minded smile conveyed to Natasha and Sonya his fiancee's invitation to the wedding, and went away. Natasha with a gay, flirtatious smile talked to him and congratulated on his approaching wedding the same Boris with whom she had formerly been in love. In the state of intoxication she was in, everything seemed simple and natural.
The scantily clad Helene smiled at everyone in the same way, and Natasha gave Boris a similar smile.
Helene's box was filled and surrounded from the stalls by the most distinguished and intellectual men, who seemed to compete with one another in their wish to let everyone see that they knew her.

During the whole intermission, Kuragin stood with Dolokhov in front of the orchestra rail, looking at the Rostovs' box. Natasha knew he was talking about her, and this pleased her. She even turned so that he could see her profile in what she thought was its most flattering angle. Before the second act began, Pierre appeared in the stalls. The Rostovs had not seen him since their arrival. His face looked sad, and he had grown even stouter since Natasha last saw him. He walked up to the front rows, not noticing anyone. Anatole went up to him and began speaking, looking at and pointing to the Rostovs' box. On seeing Natasha, Pierre brightened and, hastily passing between the rows, came toward their box. When he reached it, he leaned on his elbows and, smiling, talked to her for a long time. While she was conversing with Pierre, Natasha heard a man's voice in Countess Bezukhova's box and somehow knew it was Kuragin. She turned and their eyes met. Almost smiling, he gazed straight into her eyes with such an enraptured, adoring look that it seemed strange to be so near him, to look at him like that, to be so sure he admired her, and not to know him.

In the second act there was scenery representing tombstones, there was a round hole in the canvas representing the moon, shades were raised over the footlights, and from horns and double basses came deep notes while many people appeared from the right and left wearing black cloaks and holding things like daggers in their hands. They began waving their arms. Then some other people ran in and began dragging away the girl who had been in white and was now in light blue. They didn't drag her off at once, but sang with her for a long time and then finally dragged her off, and behind the scenes something metallic was struck three times and everyone knelt down and sang a prayer. All this was repeatedly interrupted by the enthusiastic shouts of the audience.

During this act, every time Natasha looked toward the stalls she saw Anatole Kuragin with his arm thrown across the back of his chair, staring at her. She was pleased to see that he was captivated by her, and it didn't occur to her that there was anything wrong in it.

When the second act was over, Countess Bezukhova rose, turned toward the Rostovs' box — her bosom fully exposed — beckoned the old count with a gloved finger, and paying no attention to those who had entered her box, began talking to him with a charming smile.
"Do introduce me to your lovely daughters," she said. "The whole town is singing their praises and I don't even know them!"
Natasha rose and curtsied to the splendid countess. She was so pleased by praise from this brilliant beauty that she blushed with pleasure.
"I want to become a Muscovite too, now," said Helene. "How is it you're not ashamed to bury such pearls in the country?"
Countess Bezukhova fully deserved her reputation as a fascinating woman. She could say what she didn't think — especially what was flattering — quite simply and naturally.

"Dear count, you must let me look after your daughters! Though I'm not staying here long this time — nor are you — I'll try to give them a good time. I had already heard a lot about you in Petersburg and wanted to get to know you," she said to Natasha with her perfect, lovely smile. "I'd heard about you from my page, Drubetskoy. Have you heard he's getting married? And also from my husband's friend Bolkonsky, Prince Andrew Bolkonsky," she went on with special emphasis, implying that she knew about his relationship to Natasha. To get better acquainted she asked that one of the young ladies should come into her box for the rest of the performance, and Natasha moved over to it.

The scene of the third act represented a palace in which many candles were burning and pictures of knights with short beards hung on the walls. In the middle stood what were probably a king and a queen. The king waved his right arm and, clearly nervous, sang something badly and sat down on a crimson throne. The girl who had been first in white and then in light blue now wore only a shift, and stood beside the throne with her hair down. She sang something mournfully, addressing the queen, but the king waved his arm severely, and men and women with bare legs came in from both sides and began dancing together. Then the violins played very shrilly and merrily, and one of the women with thick bare legs and thin arms, separating from the others, went behind the wings, adjusted her bodice, returned to the middle of the stage, and began jumping and striking one foot rapidly against the other. In the stalls everyone clapped and shouted "bravo!" Then one of the men went into a corner of the stage. The cymbals and horns in the orchestra struck up more loudly, and this man with bare legs jumped very high and waved his feet about very rapidly. (He was Duport, who earned sixty thousand rubles a year for this skill.) Everyone in the stalls, boxes, and galleries began clapping and shouting with all their might, and the man stopped and began smiling and bowing to all sides. Then other men and women danced with bare legs. Then the king again shouted to the sound of music, and they all began singing. But suddenly a storm came on, chromatic scales and diminished sevenths were heard in the orchestra, everyone ran off, again dragging one of their number away, and the curtain dropped. Once more there was a tremendous noise among the audience, and with rapturous faces everyone began shouting: "Duport! Duport! Duport!" Natasha no longer thought this strange. She looked around with pleasure, smiling joyfully.
"Isn't Duport delightful?" Helene asked her.
"Oh, yes," replied Natasha.
